cctv.faq.3: My CCTV files are .ps — will this work?
cctv.faq.4: Yes. Most Chinese DVRs (Xiongmai, HiSilicon and white-label rebrands) wrap MPEG‐PS in a proprietary header starting with the bytes IMKH. CCTV Converter detects that signature and converts to MP4 with no quality loss in seconds.
cctv.faq.5: What about Dahua .dav or Hikvision files?
cctv.faq.6: Dahua DHAV files convert directly. Hikvision is more varied — standard H.264 backups work fine; encrypted backups (.crypt) cannot be decrypted by any third-party tool and need Hikvision's own player.
cctv.faq.7: Does it really keep all the original quality?
cctv.faq.8: Yes. The default conversion is a stream copy, meaning the video and audio packets are repackaged into MP4 without being decoded or re-encoded. The output is bit-identical in quality to the source. Re-encoding only happens as a fallback if the original stream is incompatible with MP4, and it uses high-quality H.264.
cctv.faq.9: Can I burn the date and time into the video?
cctv.faq.10: Yes — tick “Add timestamp overlay to converted video” in the options panel before you convert. A date/time clock taken from each file’s recording time is burned into the bottom-left of the MP4, incrementing per frame. Required by most insurance companies and accepted as evidence by courts in many jurisdictions. (See our Terms on relying on output as a sole legal record.)
cctv.faq.11: Can I edit or trim clips?
cctv.faq.12: Yes. The built-in editor lets you trim to the exact frame, crop, rotate, and adjust brightness, contrast, saturation, sharpness and gamma, apply one-tap look presets, reduce night-time grain, and set the output resolution and quality. You can save your settings as presets, and automatically blur or black out faces for privacy. Edits always export to a new MP4 — your original files are never modified.
cctv.faq.13: Can I watch several cameras at once?
cctv.faq.14: Yes — the Multi-Camera view plays up to six recordings side by side on a single timeline, with per-camera offset nudging so you can line up clocks that have drifted apart. Snapshot every angle at once, build a contact sheet, or export a synchronized composite video.
cctv.faq.15: How do the motion highlights work?
cctv.faq.16: Point the app at your footage and it scans for movement, then exports just the clips where something happens — with adjustable sensitivity and pre/post-roll padding so you keep the run-up and run-out of each event. Save each event separately or as one combined highlight reel, and skip hours of an empty driveway.
cctv.faq.18: Around 200× realtime for a typical CCTV bitrate. A 30-second clip converts in well under a second. With parallel conversion enabled (up to 8 files at once), a full day of recordings — a few hundred clips — takes well under a minute on a normal laptop. Optional GPU acceleration (NVIDIA / Intel / AMD) speeds up re-encodes. Stop and resume any time.

The app auto-detects your Windows language on first launch and you can switch any time from the globe icon in the toolbar.
cctv.faq.22: Yes. CCTV Converter does its work entirely on your machine and never uploads your footage. Once installed you can disconnect from the internet and it keeps working — the only optional network use is checking for an update when you ask it to.
cctv.faq.24: Windows 10 or Windows 11, x64. The Microsoft Store version is self-contained — it bundles the .NET runtime and ffmpeg, so there are no prerequisites to install and no admin rights are needed for normal use.

cctv.help.15: Install from the Microsoft Store and launch the app. Then:
cctv.help.16: Pick a source — drag a folder (or your DVR's SD card) onto the window, or click Browse next to "Source folder". The app walks any date subfolders and lists every video file it finds.
cctv.help.17: Pick an output folder — where converted MP4s are written. Your last-used source and output folders are remembered for next time.
cctv.help.18: Filter and select — narrow the list by duration, date, time of day or filename, then tick the files (or whole days) you want.
cctv.help.19: Everything runs on your own machine; nothing is uploaded.
cctv.help.21: Tick the files you want and click Convert selected. Where the source stream is already MP4-compatible the app does a stream copy (no re-encoding, no quality loss, near-instant); otherwise it re-encodes to clean H.264.
cctv.help.22: Parallel conversion — convert up to 8 files at once (set in Settings). A full day of clips finishes in seconds on a multi-core PC.
cctv.help.23: Encoder — choose Auto, CPU, or a specific GPU (NVIDIA / Intel / AMD) in Settings. Auto detects the best available and silently falls back to CPU if a GPU encode fails.
cctv.help.24: Date/time burn-in — tick "Add timestamp overlay" to burn a per-frame clock into the bottom-left of the output, useful for insurance or incident reports.
cctv.help.25: Merge — combine a day's clips, or any selection, into one continuous MP4 in chronological order.
cctv.help.26: CSV export — export the file list (name, size, duration, resolution, format, timestamps) for cataloguing.
cctv.help.27: Optional cleanup — "Delete source files after successful conversion" reclaims space as you go (with confirmation).
cctv.help.29: Select a converted clip and click Edit to open the in-place editor. From there you can:
cctv.help.30: Trim — set the start and end points (down to a single frame) with the range slider or the I/O shortcuts, and mark multiple segments to export separately or merged.
cctv.help.31: Crop & rotate — crop to a region of interest or rotate footage that was recorded sideways.
cctv.help.32: Image adjustments — brightness, contrast, saturation, sharpness and gamma, with a live preview, plus one-tap look presets (Night, Bright, Clarify, Vivid, Black & White) shown as thumbnails.
cctv.help.33: Noise reduction — Off / Light / Medium / Strong, to clean up grainy night footage.
cctv.help.34: Output size & quality — pick a resolution and quality level for the exported file.
cctv.help.35: Presets — save a combination of edit settings and reapply it in one click.
cctv.help.36: Exports are written to a new MP4 — your original files are never modified. A progress bar (with cancel) shows the export as it runs.
cctv.help.38: Tick two or more converted clips and click Multi View to open up to six cameras side by side on a shared timeline. You can:
cctv.help.39: Nudge each camera's sync offset to line up clocks that have drifted apart.
cctv.help.40: Rename and rearrange cells, and solo a cell to hear its audio.
cctv.help.41: Snapshot all cameras at once, or build a combined contact sheet.
cctv.help.42: Export a synchronized composite video of the whole grid.
cctv.help.44: Select footage and choose Detect motion to have the app scan for movement and extract only the clips where something happens.
cctv.help.45: Sensitivity — Low / Medium / High controls how much movement counts as an event.
cctv.help.46: Pre/post-roll — keep a few seconds before and after each event so nothing is clipped.
cctv.help.47: Output — save each event as its own file, or stitch them all into a single highlight reel.
cctv.help.48: Review — optionally review and deselect false positives before anything is written.
cctv.help.49: Results are cached, so changing the pre/post-roll and re-exporting doesn't repeat the scan.
cctv.help.51: In the preview, a thumbnail filmstrip sits above the seek bar for fast scrubbing, and hovering the bar shows a preview pop-up. After a motion scan, a heatmap is painted along the seek bar so you can jump straight to the busy moments; use the prev/next-motion buttons to hop between events.
cctv.help.53: Turn on Watch source folder in Settings and the app monitors that folder, automatically converting new recordings as they appear — a hands-off workflow for an always-on DVR. It waits until each file has finished being written before converting, and can pop a notification when a batch completes.
cctv.help.57: A few formats are genuinely undecodable by any third-party tool — most notably Hikvision encrypted backups (.crypt), which need Hikvision's own player. Standard Hikvision H.264 backups convert fine.
cctv.help.58: A file won't convert because it's "in use"
cctv.help.59: Another program (Windows' Films & TV, an Explorer preview, or antivirus) may be holding the file. Close any preview windows and try again; the app retries automatically for a few seconds.
cctv.help.60: The preview won't play a source file
cctv.help.61: Some raw CCTV formats can't be previewed until converted. Convert the file first, then preview or edit the MP4.
cctv.help.62: Where are my settings and logs?
cctv.help.63: Open About → Open log/data folder, or browse to %LOCALAPPDATA%\CctvConverter\. It holds your config, the thumbnail cache and an error log — handy if you ever need to send a support report.
cctv.help.65: The Microsoft Store edition updates automatically. You can also choose About → Check for updates at any time. The app makes no other network requests; see the Privacy Policy for details.
cctv.help.66: Still stuck? Email info@davidarthur.app and we'll help. If the app saved you a headache, you can buy us a coffee — entirely optional.
cctv.help.68: In the editor, click Detect faces to automatically find and follow faces across the clip, then hide the ones you choose. Everything runs on your PC — nothing is uploaded.
cctv.help.69: Detect & track — faces are found and followed as they move, each with a box that tracks it frame by frame.
cctv.help.70: Choose who to hide — click a box to keep that person visible or to redact them; only the faces you pick are hidden.
cctv.help.71: Blackout, pixelate or blur — choose how hidden areas look.
cctv.help.72: Draw your own & track it — draw a box over anything — a number plate, a person, a screen — and click Track this area to make the box follow its subject automatically. If the subject appears at other times too, draw another box there.
cctv.help.73: Automatic detection is a helpful first pass, not a guarantee — always play the clip back and cover anything left exposed before sharing.

cctv.help.81: Right-click a day of recordings and choose Play as timeline to watch the whole day's files as one continuous video — scrub across the joins, jump between motion events across the day, and export any span without opening each file separately.
